title: Loops and record-safe input: retrieval check
markdown:
## Recall before you check

This retrieval pass revisits loops over lines and files without re-teaching them. Before opening the check, say in your own words why `while IFS= read -r line` is the record-safe way to read lines, what `for f in *.log` does when no file matches and how `shopt -s nullglob` changes it, why `for x in $(cat file)` breaks on spaces, and how `find -print0` pairs with `read -d ''` to loop over awkward filenames.

## What to bring back

- `while IFS= read -r line; do …; done < file` keeps leading whitespace and backslashes intact and reads exactly one line per iteration.
- `read -r` disables backslash interpretation; without `-r`, `\n` inside a line is mangled.
- `for f in *.log` iterates matching names; with no match the literal pattern is used unless `nullglob` is set.
- `for x in $(cat file)` splits on all whitespace and expands globs; it is not a line loop.
- `find . -print0 | while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do …; done` handles spaces and newlines in names.
- A `while read` loop in a pipeline runs in a subshell, so variables set inside it are not visible afterwards; use `done < <(cmd)` to keep them.

Answer from memory first, then read the feedback.

key_takeaways: while IFS= read -r is the record-safe line loop.
nullglob makes an unmatched pattern expand to nothing instead of itself.
Loops fed by a pipeline run in a subshell; use process substitution to keep variables.

questions.prompt: Which loop reads a file one line at a time, preserving leading spaces and backslashes?
choices: for line in $(cat file); do …; done
while IFS= read -r line; do …; done < file
while read line; do …; done < file
for line in file; do …; done
questions.correct_answer: while IFS= read -r line; do …; done < file
questions.explanation: IFS= keeps leading whitespace; -r keeps backslashes; the redirection supplies the file.

questions.prompt: With no matching files, what does `for f in *.log; do echo "$f"; done` print by default?
questions.explanation: An unmatched glob stays literal unless nullglob is set.

questions.prompt: Why is `for x in $(cat names.txt)` wrong for names containing spaces?
choices: cat cannot be used in loops
The unquoted substitution is split on all whitespace, so one name becomes several words
questions.correct_answer: The unquoted substitution is split on all whitespace, so one name becomes several words
questions.explanation: Word splitting applies to unquoted command substitution; it also expands globs.
questions.learning_objective: Explain why unquoted substitution splits records

questions.prompt: Which pairing loops over filenames that may contain spaces or newlines safely?
questions.explanation: NUL-delimited names with read -d '' are the only fully safe form.

questions.prompt: A counter incremented inside `cat file | while read -r line; do ((n++)); done` is 0 afterwards. Why?
choices: The loop ran in a subshell because it is part of a pipeline
questions.correct_answer: The loop ran in a subshell because it is part of a pipeline
questions.explanation: Use done < file or done < <(cmd) so the loop runs in the current shell.
questions.learning_objective: Keep loop variables out of a subshell
